title: Λαγωοὶ καὶ ἀλώπεκες
part: The Hares and the Foxes (Chambry 190 · Perry 256)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 190 (= Perry 256). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λαγωοί ποτε πολεμοῦντες ἀετοῖς παρεκάλουν εἰς συμμαχίαν ἀλώπεκας.
sentences.tr: Lagōoi pote polemountes aetois parekaloun eis symmachian alōpekas.
sentences.l: Hares once, being at war with eagles, were calling foxes into alliance.
sentences.i: Hares once at war with eagles called on the foxes to join them as allies.
sentences.n: πολεμέω takes the dative of the enemy fought, not an accusative object. παρακαλέω εἰς is to summon a man into a thing — here into a συμμαχία, a fighting alliance.

sentences.t: Αἱ δὲ ἔφησαν· « Ἐβοηθήσαμεν ἂν ὑμῖν, εἰ μὴ ᾔδειμεν τίνες ἐστὲ καὶ τίσι πολεμεῖτε. »
sentences.tr: Hai de ephēsan· « Eboēthēsamen an hymin, ei mē ēideimen tines este kai tisi polemeite. »
sentences.l: But they said: « We would have helped you, if we did not know who you are and with whom you are at war. »
sentences.n: The unreal condition is mixed. ἄν with the aorist indicative makes the main clause past and unfulfilled, "we would have helped"; ᾔδειμεν is a pluperfect in form, but οἶδα is a perfect with present meaning, so its pluperfect carries imperfect force, "we knew" — the protasis therefore bears on now. βοηθέω takes the dative of the party helped. The refusal insults twice over: the foxes know both what the hares are and what they have taken on.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ φιλονεικοῦντες τοῖς κρείττοσι τῆς ἑαυτῶν σωτηρίας καταφρονοῦσι.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hoi philoneikountes tois kreittosi tēs heautōn sōtērias kataphronousi.
sentences.l: The story shows that those who contend with their betters think nothing of their own safety.
sentences.n: φιλονεικέω, "to be fond of strife", takes the dative of the party quarrelled with; καταφρονέω takes the genitive of what is looked down on. οἱ κρείττονες are simply the stronger, the party with the advantage.
